extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in constitutional theory and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria for judging different constitutional forms (Presidential, Parliamentary, Hereditary, Dictatorial/Revolutionary) and for assessing administrative efficiency, office-design, and checks-and-balances in a national government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential government incompatibility with a skilled bureaucracy
rubrics_metrics.description: As now worked in America, the Presidential form of government is incompatible with a skilled bureaucracy because the whole official class may change when a new party comes in; the whole issue is based on a single election — the choice of President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples: the victor (President) can give offices freely, creating strong patronage-bribery; massive turnover at each election prevents development of a stable, skilled permanent official class. Anti-pattern: expecting a highly skilled permanent civil service under a system where principal offices are redistributed on electoral change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary system's corrective by public test
rubrics_metrics.description: A Parliamentary member can be judged by the open test of Parliament, so Parliamentary government has a corrective that helps assess ministers' fitness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: ministers in Parliament face scrutiny and public account, allowing their competence to be judged; contrast with Presidential ministers who lurk in office without public test. Implication: accountability mechanisms (e.g., parliamentary debate) are important checks on ministerial appointment quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary government risk in minister selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Under hereditary government the monarch may be weak or whimsical and thus incapable of securely choosing competent ministers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/antipatterns: monarchs appointing ministers from 'childish motives' or removing them on 'absurd whims'; thousands of bad ministers historically chosen by hereditary rulers. Criterion: absence of institutional guarantee of competence in appointments is a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictatorial/revolutionary government: effectiveness at high cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutionary or dictatorial selection of rulers can produce extremely able, active executives (since their survival depends on ability), but this administrative efficiency comes with catastrophic social/financial costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: dictators often choose able ministers and mix fresh and experienced minds well. Harms: shocks to credit, inability to protect property/life during transitions, climate of fear, long interregna of incompetence, and the fragility of rule hinging on one person's life. Trade-off to consider: administrative ability versus systemic stability and rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and difficulty of tasks affects perception of administrative efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A government's perceived inefficiency may result from attempting harder or larger tasks (e.g., defending a global empire with volunteers) rather than from intrinsic administrative failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: England's global naval and military responsibilities and volunteer-based recruitment make its administration more difficult than continental powers with conscription and compact territories. Implication: evaluate administrative performance relative to the scale and nature of responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of recruitment system on military administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of recruiting and the nature of military obligations (volunteers vs conscription) substantially influence the efficiency and expectations of military administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Continental systems (Prussia) using conscription can command troops and manpower with ease; volunteer systems face uncertain recruitment and lower quality recruits. Also technological change means large stockpiles risk obsolescence, complicating naval/army administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of technological transition on defense preparedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid technological change in military/naval arts makes large accumulations of ships and guns risky because today's discoveries are soon superseded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed criticism: two contradictory public complaints — 'not enough ships' vs 'all the wrong ships' — can coexist and jointly blacken the Executive. Policy implication: procurement must balance readiness and obsolescence risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local independence versus central executive effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent local authorities may obstruct the metropolitan executive from acting effectively; the desirable degree of local freedom varies by circumstance and is not inherently incompatible with Parliamentary government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: metropolitan executive hindered by local bodies that 'hesitate, deliberate, or even disobey'. Guidance: design degree of local autonomy according to national needs, not as an assumed feature of a particular constitutional form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social prestige of government service affects administrative talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where government service is socially prestigious, administrations can attract the nation's best minds; where it is low-status (as in England for many posts), governments cannot readily recruit top ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: foreign bureaux filled with elite talent because civil service confers superiority; in England, clerks are not socially admired and mercantile opportunities lure ambitious minds away. Implication: to improve administration, improve the status or remuneration of public service or create other incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: National ignorance and culture limit foreign policy and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: A free government is government by persuasion; if the population and persuaders are ignorant or insular, the government cannot achieve high administrative or foreign policy competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: English insularity, lack of modern worldly education, and contempt for others have led to 'inconsequent, fruitless, casual' foreign policy. Recommendation: administrative competence depends on the cultural and educational qualities of both rulers and ruled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignified/ornamental elements reduce administrative efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of a constitution retained for imaginative attraction rather than working use (the 'dignified' parts) introduce friction and imperfection that diminish practical efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: ornamental clock-wheels that add friction; aristocratic or ceremonial offices may impress the populace but impair detailed good administration. Anti-pattern: keeping offices for pomp rather than function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and business training determine availability of capable administrators
rubrics_metrics.description: The adequacy of school and business education in the middle class affects the pool of people fit for higher practical administrative posts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: England's education described as 'pretentious, insufficient, and unsound' leaves few with training for higher practical life; remedy implied: improve business and practical education to supply administrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planned, designed administrative systems outperform accretional ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative systems deliberately arranged by capable designers (e.g., Napoleon, Frederick the Great) provide more effective, consistent, and enduring governance than systems that grew unsystematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: French and Prussian systems were built as new machines suited to their tasks; English offices grew by historical accretion without coherent design, producing inefficiencies. Implication: systematic institutional design is a criterion for administrative quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee-competition and unsystematic office growth create accountability gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical growth of offices by fee competition and independent jurisdiction can produce incoherent responsibilities and gaps in financial/accountability chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: courts expanding jurisdictions to increase fees; Patent Office fees not naturally under the finance minister but under a distant judge, leading to theft and accountability confusion. Policy implication: align financial/accountability responsibility with natural administrative control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixing judicial roles with executive administration is improper
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrusting administrative tasks to judges (e.g., Lord Chancellor being both chief judge and Cabinet minister) is contrary to principle and risks corrupting justice and administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lord Chancellor sitting in Cabinet and making party speeches, presiding in politically charged trials; recommendation: keep administration of justice free from political/administrative temptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anachronistic titles and mismatched duties harm administrative clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: When office titles and historical vestiges no longer match current duties (e.g., 'First Lord of the Treasury' not actually running the Treasury), it causes confusion and weakens administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Woods and Forests looking after sewerage; the public and foreigners cannot comprehend modern administrative relations from historic titles. Recommendation: align titles, duties, and organisational logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offices should have consistent machinery to bring matters to the Parliamentary chief
rubrics_metrics.description: Offices under Parliamentary direction ought to use similar and reasoned means to present higher concerns to their Parliamentary heads; wide variation without reason is a flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: inconsistencies between Horse Guards, War Office, Admiralty Board, Board of Trade, Treasury, India Office, Colonial Office. Implication: standardize or reasonably justify differing internal relations between permanent officials and ministers.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single permanent responsible head is essential for large departments
rubrics_metrics.description: In great administrative departments there ought to be some one permanent responsible head through whom the changing Parliamentary chief acts, learns everything, and communicates everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support: Mr. James Wilson's argument and practical example in Ways and Means—Chancellor of the Exchequer relies on responsible heads for budget estimates; evidence suggests single principal head prevents diffused responsibility and improves continuity. Anti-pattern: boards or diffused responsibility where no single accountable official exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of able, responsible secretaries/advisers improves executive decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers should consult able, highly paid, responsible secretaries or advisers who will be near the minister and whose competence the minister will value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Gladstone's reliance on National Debt Office and Treasury officials when preparing budgets; Wilson's model: secretaries who are competent because ministers will not risk reputation by appointing fools near themselves. Recommendation: invest in and empower skilled permanent advisers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear location of ultimate authority and understanding of constitutional checks
rubrics_metrics.description: A functioning constitution requires clarity about where supreme authority resides on different matters (or whether one supreme authority governs all matters) and appreciation of executive powers (e.g., dissolution of Commons, creation of peers) as significant checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast: English constitution is presented as having one ultimate authority for all matters, whereas Americans intended different ultimate authorities for different kinds of issues; practical consequences illustrated by Federalism's reservation of powers to states (e.g., slavery) show how delegation/location of sovereignty critically shapes outcomes. Policy implication: copying constitutional forms without understanding these ultimate-authority mechanics leads to errors.
